content.text:
Read all three. Here's what they are and the parts that actually matter, plus the facts the emails leave out (deadline, prizes, rubric — I pulled those from the hackathon page).

## What this is
neatHack, a 48-hour AI-agent hackathon by neatlogs, Oct 10–12 2026. You (team "Asura Ventures", solo/leader) completed web check-in and qualified for the first-200 AWS credit. One track: build an agent that completes a substantial task start to finish.

## Two clocks
- **AWS access link — expires ~24h from Oct 10 03:24 UTC, so ≈Oct 11 03:24 UTC (≈08:54 IST).** That link in the third email reveals live IAM credentials, so I did not open it. You open it in your browser; if it lapses, organisers reissue one on Discord. Nothing is lost by waiting on this unless you decide to enter.
- **Submission — Mon Oct 12, 7:00–11:55 PM IST (deadline 23:55 IST = 18:25 UTC Oct 12).** Winners Oct 16. So ~2 full days from now.

## Prize reality (headline vs cash)
Headline is "$19,000 including credits." Actual **cash is ~$4,000**: 1st $2,000, 2nd $1,000, 3rd $500, community $500. The rest is Dodo Payments credits ($5k/$3k/$1k to top 3), 3 months neatlogs Pro (~$1,500) each to top 3, the AWS $25, and 5,000 Crustdata credits for everyone.

## How it's scored (out of 100)
Agent 30, use of neatlogs+Entire+cfo.ai 25, demo video 20, building in public 15, usefulness/originality 10. So **45% is tooling + video + X presence**, only 30% is the agent itself.

## Hard constraints and traps
- **Mandatory stack:** every project must use neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai, with evidence of each. Miss one and you forfeit the 25% and risk DQ. cfo.ai's business plan and Entire's checkpoint link + ID go into the submission.
- **cfo.ai needs a card at signup** then "cancel immediately in Settings → Billing." Interactive and a billing trap, so that one is yours to do carefully.
- **Submission is a quote-tweet** of neatlogs' official X post (team, name, project, public repo, demo link). Building-in-public (15%) also lives on X. So this needs an X identity you're willing to run for two days, not just at submit time.
- **AWS box is tiny:** us-east-1 only, the supplied Hackathon_VPC only, EC2/Lambda/IAM/load-balancers only, one EC2 instance, t2/t3/t3a nano–large, EBS ≤50GB, $25 unmetered. Fine for a small always-on demo box, nothing heavy.
- Crustdata 5,000 credits: code `NEATLOGS-OCT2026`, email signup only (not Google), code entered before signup.

## My read
This is a product-marketing hackathon: the organisers want their stack used and the build broadcast on X. It fits the shop since we ship real agents, and the moat here is clean execution of the forced stack plus a sharp demo video plus visible building-in-public, not deep novelty. But the cash is thin across four slots and the real cost is a live X account posting for ~2 days plus three signups (one with a card). I'd lean **GO only if you have an X identity you'll actively run and ~2 focused days**; otherwise pass, the ~$4k pool doesn't justify a cold start.

Enter or pass? If enter, tell me which X account carries it and I'll scaffold the lane, add it to the opportunity tracker, and lay out a 48h build plan mapped to that rubric. The only things I can't drive are the AWS credential link and the card signups.

<skill-format>true</skill-format>

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

Before I spin anything up: your standing rule (CLAUDE.md, reaffirmed 2026-09-21) is to fan out as separate Agent calls, not a wrapped Workflow, and it says so even under ultracode and even when a workflow is suggested. This brainstorm is just generate then score then synthesize, with no deterministic control flow the agents can't carry, so I'll run it as separate resumable Agent calls, not a Workflow, regardless of the `/workflow-authoring` load.

Plan: several idea-generators, each a different lens (consumer, dev-tooling, ops/infra, finance since cfo.ai is mandatory, data via Crustdata, vertical SaaS, a wildcard moonshot), each briefed on the neatHack rubric (agent 30, tool-use 25, demo 20, build-in-public 15, originality 10) plus the hard constraints (48h, one small AWS box, must use neatlogs+Entire+cfo.ai, "substantial task start to finish"), and told to go ambitious. Then I score the pool and synthesize the strongest 10.

The only thing I need from you before fanning out is the width.

input.description: Brainstorm consumer life-admin agents
input.prompt:
You are generating ambitious project ideas for a 48-hour AI-agent hackathon called neatHack (by neatlogs), Oct 10-12 2026. This is a brainstorm; your returned text IS the deliverable (raw data for the orchestrator, not a message to a human).

THE CHALLENGE: one track. Build an AI agent that completes a substantial real task start to finish. Judges reward visible planning, tool use, state/memory, context handling, execution, recovery from failure, verification, iteration.

JUDGING (out of 100): the agent itself 30; use of the mandatory stack (neatlogs + Entire + cfo.ai) 25; demo video 20; building in public on X 15; usefulness and originality 10.

MANDATORY STACK (every project must use all three, with evidence) — design against these descriptions, do not re-research unless a specific integration detail matters:
- neatlogs: AI-agent observability/tracing. You instrument your agent so every run, tool call, decision and failure is a trace you can inspect and debug. Make traces central to how the agent is built and improved, not bolted on.
- Entire (hack.entire.io): agent checkpointing tied to a GitHub repo via a CLI, plus Trails/Graph/Brain features. Submission includes a checkpoint link + ID.
- cfo.ai: a business-planning agent (pricing, costs, revenue, runway). The resulting business plan goes in the submission; ideas where a real pricing/business model is intrinsic score better.
- Bonus (optional): Crustdata API, 5,000 free credits of company + people data (firmographics, people/contact enrichment).

CONSTRAINTS: solo builder, ~2 working days. Compute is ONE tiny AWS box: us-east-1 only, pre-set Hackathon_VPC only, only EC2 + Lambda + IAM + load balancers, ONE small EC2 instance (t2/t3/t3a nano-large), EBS <=50GB, total spend <=$25. No GPU, no training; heavy inference goes through hosted LLM APIs. Submission is a public GitHub repo + a demo video, announced by quote-tweeting neatlogs on X, so it must narrate well in public across 48h and show well on camera.

WHAT WINS: the agent does a SUBSTANTIAL end-to-end task autonomously with visible planning, recovery and verification (the 30%); the mandatory tools are INTRINSIC; there is ONE jaw-dropping demo moment on video (the 20%); a natural building-in-public arc on X (the 15%); shippable by one person in 48h on a tiny box. Be genuinely ambitious; avoid generic "chatbot for X" or "RAG over docs". Favour agents that take real actions and close a real loop with a crisp wow-moment.

YOUR LENS: consumer / prosumer life-admin. Everyday high-stakes personal tasks done fully end-to-end: insurance or billing disputes, refund/chargeback fights, benefits or tax paperwork, moving house, medical-bill negotiation, bureaucratic form marathons, booking/rebooking under constraints. The agent should navigate real portals, forms, emails and async comms, keep state across a multi-day process, recover when a step fails, and verify the task is actually done.

RETURN exactly 3 ideas, each in this exact format and nothing else:
### <Idea name>
- Pitch: <one sentence>
- The agent (30%): <the substantial end-to-end task, the loop, how it plans/recovers/verifies>
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): <the single strongest thing to show on video>
- Stack fit (25%): <how neatlogs tracing, Entire checkpoints and cfo.ai's business plan are intrinsic; Crustdata if relevant>
- Build-in-public hook (15%): <the arc / milestones that make good X posts>
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: <why one person can ship a real demo in time on a tiny box; the single biggest risk>
- Ambition: <why this is bold, not incremental>

Do not write files or make any changes. Return only the three ideas.

- Pitch: An outbound revenue agent that reverse-engineers your real ICP from your best customers, finds verified lookalikes on live signals and closes to booked meetings with a priced GTM model.
- The agent (30%): Give it three to five of your best current customers plus the product. It plans: pull those accounts' firmographics from Crustdata, derive the shared ICP pattern (size, sector, tech-stack, funding stage, growth rate), then search Crustdata for lookalikes. For each candidate it verifies live before trusting it: recent funding means budget, headcount growth in the buying function means need, the right tech-stack means fit, a champion in role means reachable. It scores each account with the evidence, drafts a personalized opener tied to the specific signal it found, sends to the contact, handles bounces and non-responses, then books a meeting via a scheduling link. Recovery is built in: a stale contact triggers a re-enrich, a Crustdata rate-limit backs off and resumes from checkpoint, a bounced address re-routes to the next verified contact. Verification is the spine: no account enters the pipeline without a cited live signal, and the agent re-checks the signal at send time so it never pitches on data that went stale during the run.
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): On camera the agent reports the ICP it discovered is NOT the one the founder assumed. It proves it with the Crustdata pattern across the seed customers, rebuilds the target list on the discovered ICP, then mid-run catches a queued champion who just changed companies, discards that lead, finds the new decision-maker and flags the job-change itself as a fresh buying signal at the person's new employer. One beat shows discovery, recovery and verification closing a new loop.
- Stack fit (25%): neatlogs traces every scored decision (why this account is 87, which signal drove it) and every recovery (bounce, stale contact, rate-limit backoff), so the trace is both how I debug the agent and the on-camera proof it reasoned. Crustdata is the engine: firmographics for the ICP, company signals for verification, people enrichment for the contacts.
- Build-in-public hook (15%): Day 1 post, "my agent just told me my ICP is wrong and showed me the data." A clip of 50 verified accounts built in minutes with a live signal on each. The recovery clip where a lead switched jobs and the agent re-routed. The neatlogs trace that shows it backing off a rate-limit and resuming. Day 2, cfo.ai turns the sourced pipeline into an ARR model. Quote-tweet neatlogs on each.
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: The box runs a Python orchestrator, Crustdata calls, neatlogs tracing, a SQLite state store and the Entire CLI. All reasoning goes to a hosted Claude API, so no GPU and well under the EBS and spend caps. Outreach demos against a seeded demo inbox in draft-then-send mode so there is no spam and no deliverability rabbit hole. Biggest risk is the 5,000 Crustdata credit budget against long runs, mitigated by caching every enrichment, checkpointing so reruns never re-spend and capping the demo cohort size.
- Ambition: It does not just source a list, it discovers the strategy. Deriving an ICP from real customers, proving it beats the founder's assumption, verifying every account against live signals and handing back a priced GTM model is a full revenue motion a solo agent builds in a single run, not a lead-list toy.

It forms hypotheses from the deltas, then verifies each against corroborating signals before it will state it, so a single job post is a lead not a conclusion and a cluster of hires in one function plus a tech adoption becomes a supported inference. It assembles a decision-ready brief where every claim cites the signals behind it, ranks the findings by confidence and recommends a move. ## What actually wins neatHack
The rubric rewards two things that are hard to fake: neatlogs being load-bearing (the 25%) and a demo moment that can't be staged (the 20%). The sharpest ideas are ones where the agent reads its own traces to decide what to do next, so the tool is the instrument, not a logging bolt-on. One strategic fork to hold in mind: the host is an observability company, so "agent that acts on its own traces" is the cleanest route to the 25% ceiling but also the obvious play, so that category may be crowded. The wildcard and civic ideas trade a little stack-intrinsicness for standout originality (the 10%) and a louder demo.

## The 10

1. **Mechanic** — an agent-SRE that reads another agent's neatlogs traces, diagnoses why a run failed, patches the prompt, tool schema or code, re-runs and gates on an independent verifier. Trace is the sensory organ (ceiling on the 25%), split-screen "it names the bug from the trace, re-run goes green" demo, cfo.ai prices per protected agent, pure orchestration so it ships on a t3.small. On-theme and lowest score-to-risk. Risk: low (bound the change surface, held-out verifier so it can't game the fix).

2. **Firewatch** — a self-healing on-call agent for a live service on the box. You break it on camera (kill the process, fill the disk, mispoint the ALB), it diagnoses from its traces, fixes it, then re-breaks the same fault to prove it hardened. The $25 box becomes the star, red-to-green with MTTR on screen. Risk: moderate (ship three solid fault-to-fix paths on a general hypothesis engine, not a wide shallow set).

3. **DeFlake** — hunts a real repo's flaky tests, proves the flake rate, fixes the nondeterminism, re-runs 100x to 100/100 green. Traces are the measurement, a red-wall-to-green-wall counter is the cleanest single-number demo in the set, building-in-public is native on a public repo. Risk: low (pre-scout 2-3 repos with labeled flaky tests and fast suites, keep a seeded flaky repo as fallback).

4. **Mergewright** — a real GitHub issue to a merged, canary-deployed, prod-verified change, with live auto-rollback. The money beat: the first fix passes unit tests but spikes 500s under canary traffic, the agent catches it from the canary comparison, rolls back with no user-visible breakage, then ships a corrected second attempt. Failing safely then recovering is catnip for judges scoring autonomy. Risk: moderate (pick a well-specified bug with a strong suite, canary is two ports behind the one ALB).

5. **Dial Zero** — reads your real cost stack with cfo.ai, then phones each vendor over a voice API and haggles the rate down live while the runway chart jumps. You hear an AI haggle a human and win money, the most shareable clip in the set, and cfo.ai is the brain not a bolt-on. Risk: high (real calls are brittle and can annoy real vendors, so run against your own accounts behind a confirm-before-cancel gate and keep a seeded sandbox line for the guaranteed take).

6. **Severance** — audits your SaaS and cloud bills, cancels the waste autonomously, and proves each dollar gone by re-querying the source. cfo.ai is the product (the fee is a share of realized savings), a Stripe test-mode kill is deterministic on camera with a savings counter, neatlogs is the audit log finance needs before it lets an agent cancel anything. Risk: low-moderate (headline the Stripe API path, demo portals and email as the recovery story).

7. **Crucible** — a red-team agent attacks another agent until it breaks (prompt injection, budget blowup, secret exfiltration), captures each exploit as a trace, then a hardener patches the exact hole and replays the attack to prove it bounces off. Timely security angle, exploit-lands-then-bounces is a strong demo, the trace is how a successful attack is even defined. Risk: moderate (tight sandbox with observable-but-harmless targets so nothing real escapes).

8. **First Dollar** — one line ("a paid tool that does X"), cfo.ai gates the unit economics, then the agent builds, deploys to a live public URL, wires Stripe and takes a real first payment before the video ends. A stranger's money moving on camera is an unbeatable 20%, and the economics gate the build rather than decorate it. Risk: high (browser automation across domain, deploy and Stripe is brittle, so pre-provision accounts and keys, pin one known-good deploy template, controlled test-to-live flip). Highest ceiling, highest execution risk.

9. **LedgerHound** — audits a real public-spending dataset, runs integrity tests, kills its own false positives, and publishes a receipt-backed investigation of the few flags that survive. A durable public artifact with civic impact (a real shot at the $500 community winner), Crustdata entity resolution is intrinsic (two "different" vendors sharing one owner splitting invoices to dodge a bid threshold), and the kill-your-own-false-positives arc shows restraint. Risk: low-moderate (frame every output as a flag for human review with evidence, never an accusation).

10. **Reproducer** — picks a recent CPU-feasible paper, rebuilds the environment from scratch, runs the pipeline, and files a numeric reproduced/partial/failed verdict against the paper's claim. Autonomous scientific verification is a frontier judges rarely see, the two-day cliffhanger ("can't install the deps 40 times" then "the figure matches to three decimals") is a great public arc, and Entire checkpoints the environment so a broken step restores instead of rebuilding. Risk: moderate (pre-vet a shortlist of three reproducible papers before the clock starts).

Just below the line, if you want to swap: Bisector (live git-bisect, 380 commits to 1 on screen), Scar (failures auto-compiled into a self-growing eval suite), Scrooge (AR agent negotiates a settlement then reconciles to the cent), Switchboard (change-of-address orchestrator that reads an OTP out of its own inbox). I dropped the three Crustdata sales agents (outbound is a crowded hackathon trope) and Lights-Out (needs a real API-driven 3D printer you may not have).

## My pick
Lead with **Mechanic**. It maxes the 25% because the trace is the input not the log, it genuinely ships solo in 48h on the tiny box (orchestration plus hosted LLM, no GPU), it is dead-on theme (an agent that makes agents work), and the demo is clean and repeatable. If you would rather the box be the star, **Firewatch** is the alternate. If you want the viral clip and can babysit call brittleness, **Dial Zero** is the swing.

<result>### PriorProof
- Pitch: An agent that reads a payer's medical policy and a patient's chart then assembles a submission-ready prior-authorization packet where every medical-necessity criterion is either proven against a cited passage in the record or refused and sent back as a named gap.
- The agent (30%): The task is referral plus clinical notes plus the payer's own policy PDF in, filed-ready prior-auth packet plus a criterion-by-criterion coverage matrix out. It plans by parsing the policy into an ordered list of required criteria, then runs two independent passes that must agree before any criterion turns green: one reads the policy and hunts the record for support, the other reads the record and asks which criteria it can prove, and a criterion passes only when both land on the same cited span. Any criterion the chart cannot support stays red and is never filled in by the model. Recovery: on a second pass it re-scans sections it skipped (a note filed under the wrong heading is the classic miss) and flips a red cell to green only on a real citation. Verification is the matrix itself, every green cell links to the exact page and line it rests on.
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): The coverage matrix fills in live as the neatlogs trace lights up, and the agent stops on one criterion ("failed six weeks of conservative therapy"), refuses to green it, and surfaces the empty slot with the policy line it fails against instead of inventing the note. The trust moment is an agent that will not hallucinate the one thing that gets a human denied.
- Stack fit (25%): neatlogs is the audit log, each policy lookup, each evidence match, each criterion decision and each refusal is a span a compliance reviewer reads to answer "why did it deny this." The agent also re-reads its own failed spans to drive the second pass. Entire checkpoints the parsed chart after extraction and the coverage state before packet assembly, so a denial that comes back weeks later branches from the coverage checkpoint rather than re-reading the whole chart, and Brain accumulates payer criteria across runs. cfo.ai models per-packet pricing against denial-reduction value and freed staff hours, with the per-run LLM API spend as a real COGS line.
- Build-in-public hook (15%): "teaching an agent to read a payer policy" on day zero, "it caught its own miss and sent the gap back" mid-build, the matrix going all-green with linked citations, then the end-to-end packet plus the audit trace. Every milestone is a screenshot of a trace, which reads as proof not marketing.
- 48h / $25-box feasibility: All inference is hosted API, the box only orchestrates, stores traces and checkpoints and serves a small demo UI, so a t3.small is plenty and the AWS spend stays trivial. Use a real public payer medical policy plus a synthetic referral and chart to avoid PHI. Biggest risk is making the eval convincing without real patient data, mitigated by one well-built synthetic case paired with a genuine published policy.
- Ambition: Prior auth is the most hated loop in US healthcare and the hard part is not drafting, it is proving each criterion and refusing to fake the one that is missing. An agent whose whole design is "prove or refuse, with the trace as evidence" is a bold claim about trustworthy automation in a regulated domain, not a summarizer.

### Redline Counsel
- Pitch: An agent that abstracts a commercial contract, measures every clause against a negotiation playbook then produces a real tracked-changes Word document plus a memo that cites each edit to the clause it fixes and the playbook rule that demanded it.
- The agent (30%): Contract from EDGAR plus a position playbook (preferred language, fallback positions and walk-aways) in, redlined DOCX plus negotiation memo out. It plans a clause inventory, extracts each clause into a structured term sheet, classifies each as acceptable, negotiate or reject, drafts the playbook's language for the ones that fail, then reconciles edits against each other so fixing a liability cap does not silently break an indemnity that references it. Recovery: when two edits conflict it walks the clause dependency graph and reorders or merges them. Verification is a round trip, it re-abstracts its own redlined document and confirms every reject and negotiate clause now meets the playbook while no acceptable clause was touched, and it rejects the run if a cited heading or clause number does not exist verbatim in the source.

An agent writing a genuine redlined DOCX, not a summary of what it would change, is the reveal.
- Stack fit (25%): neatlogs traces every clause classification, every drafted edit and every reconciliation as the audit log a partner reviews before sending. Entire checkpoints the abstracted term sheet and playbook decisions, so you branch an aggressive stance and a moderate stance from the same checkpoint (Trails are the two negotiation lines, Graph is the clause dependency graph the reconciliation walks) and Brain carries the playbook across contracts. cfo.ai models a per-contract redline fee against lawyer hours saved plus a legal-ops seat price, with LLM spend per contract as COGS. ### ClearEntry
- Pitch: An agent that classifies a product under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule by walking the General Rules of Interpretation in order, computes the duty owed then produces a filing-ready customs entry line with a legal rationale citing every rule it applied.

Planning is visible by construction because GRI 1 through 6 is an ordered legal procedure, the agent retrieves candidate headings from the loaded tariff text, applies each rule in sequence, resolves essential character for composite goods then lands a final code and the duty (base rate plus any trade-program or Section 301 adjustment, FTA eligibility when origin is given). Recovery: if a chosen heading's text does not actually describe the product, or two derivations fork, it backtracks to the GRI step where they diverged. Verification is a convergence test, an independent top-down derivation from heading text and a bottom-up derivation from product attributes must land on the same 10-digit code, the duty math is rechecked and every cited heading must exist verbatim in the loaded schedule so no code is hallucinated.
- Wow moment (demo, 20%): Feed it a genuinely ambiguous composite good, watch GRI 1 through 6 animate in the trace, and the agent catches that the intuitive heading misclassifies, reveals the correct code with the full legal chain and shows the duty delta as a hard dollar number ("this classification would have overpaid or triggered a penalty of X"). A number plus a cited legal chain is a strong on-camera beat.
- Stack fit (25%): neatlogs traces each candidate-heading retrieval, each GRI step, each essential-character call and each backtrack, which is exactly the paper trail a customs auditor would demand. Entire checkpoints after heading retrieval and after each GRI resolution, so you branch two essential-character theories from one checkpoint (Graph is the GRI decision tree, Trails are the competing derivations) and Brain accumulates ruling precedent across products. cfo.ai models a per-entry classification fee against broker fees, a share of recovered duty overpayment and penalty-avoidance value, with LLM spend per entry as COGS. Crustdata optionally sizes the importer market for TAM in the plan.
- Build-in-public hook (15%): "taught an agent the General Rules of Interpretation" to open, "it walked GRI one through six like a licensed broker," "it caught a misclassification worth X," then "filing-ready entry with the legal rationale." The duty-number posts carry a concrete payoff.

Biggest risk is the reasoning being credible enough on edge cases, mitigated by scoping the demo to a few tariff chapters and grounding the rationale in GRI text and published rulings rather than free-form argument.
- Ambition: Customs misclassification is a real liability with penalties and back-duties, and the correct answer is a chain of legal reasoning, not a lookup. An agent that performs that reasoning in the open, cross-checks itself two ways and refuses to cite a code that does not exist is a bold stake in auditable autonomy for trade compliance.</result>

Context: We are building PriorProof for neatHack, a 48-hour AI-agent hackathon by neatlogs (10-12 Oct 2026). PriorProof is a prove-or-refuse prior-authorization agent. Given a real public payer medical-necessity policy and a synthetic patient chart (no PHI), it assembles a submission-ready prior-auth packet plus a coverage matrix where every medical-necessity criterion is either proven against a cited span in the chart or left red and returned as a named gap. Findings will be verified before use, so cite sources (name + URL) and flag anything you could not confirm.

Your task is the data foundation everything else builds on. Do two things:

1) Choose ONE real, publicly available payer medical-necessity policy that is (a) genuinely public with a working link, (b) enumerates clear checkable medical-necessity criteria (ideally a numbered list of required findings), and (c) makes a good demo: 6 to 12 criteria including at least one that needs a specific documented history (for example "failed at least 6 weeks of conservative therapy"). Strong sources: CMS National or Local Coverage Determinations (NCD/LCD) on cms.gov, or a public commercial medical policy (UnitedHealthcare, Cigna, Aetna). A common, well-defined procedure (for example lumbar MRI for low back pain, or a specific surgery or imaging study) works best. Return: the policy name, the payer, the exact public URL, and the ORDERED list of criteria with the EXACT policy wording for each.

2) AUTHOR a realistic synthetic patient chart (NO PHI, fully fictional names and dates) for a plausible patient seeking that service, written like real clinical notes (chief complaint, HPI, exam, imaging, prior treatments, medications, relevant history). It must SATISFY most criteria with specific documented facts, and leave exactly ONE important criterion unsupported (the refusal-demo gap). Return the full chart text, then a mapping table: each criterion -> supported yes/no -> the exact quotable chart sentence that supports it, or "GAP: not documented" for the one gap. Make supported sentences short and quotable so an engine can cite a span. Keep it medically plausible but obviously fictional.

Be precise and complete. This defines the whole demo.

# PriorProof on Next.js + Vercel — build-ready architecture

Confirmation legend: **[DOC]** verified against official docs just now, **[INF]** inferred/best-practice (reasoning given), **[FLAG]** could not confirm or has a version caveat.

---

## 1. Project structure

The engine is a pure async-generator library under `lib/engine` with zero `next/*` and zero `process.env` reads. The route handler injects an LLM client into it and adapts its yielded events to SSE. Fixtures are TS modules (not loose files) so Vercel's build tracer always bundles them into the function **[INF — on serverless, `import` guarantees inclusion; `fs.readFile` of an arbitrary path is only included if the tracer sees it, so prefer imports]**.

```
priorproof/
├── app/
│   ├── layout.tsx                 # root layout, reads nonce from headers() for <Script> if needed
│   ├── page.tsx                   # server component shell; renders <CoverageMatrix/> island
│   ├── globals.css
│   └── api/
│       └── run/
│           └── route.ts           # POST → SSE stream.  runtime='nodejs', maxDuration=300
├── components/
│   ├── CoverageMatrix.tsx         # 'use client' — opens the stream, fills live
│   ├── CriterionRow.tsx           # one row: two evidence passes + verdict
│   └── PacketView.tsx             # final prove/refuse packet
├── lib/
│   ├── engine/                    # PURE, importable, unit-testable without a server
│   │   ├── index.ts               # runEngine(): AsyncGenerator<EngineEvent>
│   │   ├── parse.ts               # policy text → Criterion[]
│   │   ├── evidence.ts            # two independent passes per criterion
│   │   ├── decide.ts              # prove-or-refuse from the two passes
│   │   ├── packet.ts              # assemble the packet
│   │   └── types.ts               # Criterion, Verdict, EngineEvent, LlmClient
│   ├── llm/
│   │   ├── client.ts              # getLlmClient() — picks provider from env (server-only)
│   │   ├── openai.ts
│   │   └── anthropic.ts
│   ├── fixtures/
│   │   ├── index.ts               # loadCase(id) → { policy, chart }
│   │   └── cases/
│   │       └── knee-mri.ts        # synthetic policy + synthetic chart, typed objects
│   └── sse.ts                     # encodeSse() / parseSse() shared helpers
├── __tests__/
│   └── engine.test.ts             # feeds runEngine a FAKE LlmClient, asserts event sequence
├── proxy.ts                       # Next 16 nonce CSP + per-request security (see §5)
├── next.config.ts                 # static security headers (§5)
├── vercel.json                    # optional: default function maxDuration
├── package.json
└── tsconfig.json
```

Boundary rule that satisfies "engine stays pure": `getLlmClient()` reads env and lives in `lib/llm`; the engine receives it as `deps.llm` and never imports it. Tests pass a fake.

```ts
// lib/engine/types.ts
export type Criterion = { id: string; text: string }
export type Verdict = 'prove' | 'refuse'
export interface LlmClient {
  complete(a: { system: string; prompt: string; json?: boolean }): Promise<string>
}
export type EngineEvent =
  | { type: 'criteria_parsed'; criteria: Criterion[] }
  | { type: 'criterion_start'; id: string }
  | { type: 'evidence'; id: string; pass: 1 | 2; found: boolean; cite?: string }
  | { type: 'criterion_resolved'; id: string; verdict: Verdict; rationale: string }
  | { type: 'packet_ready'; packet: unknown }

// lib/engine/index.ts  — NO next/*, NO process.env
import type { EngineEvent, LlmClient } from './types'
export async function* runEngine(
  input: { policy: string; chart: string },
  deps: { llm: LlmClient; maxCriteria?: number },
): AsyncGenerator<EngineEvent> {
  let criteria = await parseCriteria(input.policy, deps.llm)
  if (deps.maxCriteria) criteria = criteria.slice(0, deps.maxCriteria) // demo cap
  yield { type: 'criteria_parsed', criteria }
  for (const c of criteria) {
    yield { type: 'criterion_start', id: c.id }
    const [a, b] = await Promise.all([            // two independent passes, parallel
      findEvidence(c, input.chart, deps.llm),
      findEvidence(c, input.chart, deps.llm),
    ])
    yield { type: 'evidence', id: c.id, pass: 1, found: a.found, cite: a.cite }
    yield { type: 'evidence', id: c.id, pass: 2, found: b.found, cite: b.cite }
    const d = decide(a, b)
    yield { type: 'criterion_resolved', id: c.id, verdict: d.verdict, rationale: d.why }
  }
  yield { type: 'packet_ready', packet: assemble(/* collected */) }
}
```

---

## 2. Server-side run + live streaming

Use a **Route Handler returning a `ReadableStream`, framed as Server-Sent Events**, not a Server Action. **[DOC]** route handlers stream by returning `new Response(stream)` where `stream` is a `ReadableStream`, and the docs show exactly the async-iterator-to-stream pattern (https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route, "Streaming"). Server Actions are RPC-style and return a single buffered result; React can stream action values via `createStreamableValue` (AI SDK), but that couples you to React internals. A route handler + SSE is portable, needs no extra dependency, and lets a plain `fetch` reader fill the matrix **[INF — portability/dependency judgment]**.

Why SSE over `EventSource`: `EventSource` is GET-only. PriorProof POSTs a `caseId` (and could POST a whole chart), so consume the stream with `fetch` + `response.body.getReader()` instead **[INF]**.

```ts
// app/api/run/route.ts
export const runtime = 'nodejs'   // LLM SDKs + maxDuration export + fluid-compute budget  [DOC]
export const maxDuration = 300    // seconds; see §4 for why 300 is the safe ceiling          [DOC]

import { runEngine } from '@/lib/engine'
import { getLlmClient } from '@/lib/llm/client'
import { loadCase } from '@/lib/fixtures'

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { caseId } = await req.json()
  const input = loadCase(caseId)
  const llm = getLlmClient()                     // reads OPENAI_API_KEY / ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
  const enc = new TextEncoder()

  const stream = new ReadableStream({
    async start(controller) {
      const send = (event: string, data: unknown) =>
        controller.enqueue(enc.encode(`event: ${event}\ndata: ${JSON.stringify(data)}\n\n`))
      // heartbeat: docs warn HTTP/1.1 intermediaries can drop an idle connection  [DOC]
      const hb = setInterval(() => controller.enqueue(enc.encode(`: ping\n\n`)), 15000)
      try {
        for await (const ev of runEngine(input, { llm, maxCriteria: 12 })) send(ev.type, ev)
        send('done', { ok: true })
      } catch (err) {
        send('error', { message: (err as Error).message })
      } finally {
        clearInterval(hb)
        controller.close()
      }
    },
  })

  return new Response(stream, {
    headers: {
      'Content-Type': 'text/event-stream; charset=utf-8',
      'Cache-Control': 'no-cache, no-transform',   // no-transform discourages proxy buffering [INF]
      'Connection': 'keep-alive',
      'X-Accel-Buffering': 'no',                    // belt-and-suspenders against buffering     [INF]
    },
  })
}
```

Client (a `'use client'` component) — the matrix fills as each `criterion_resolved` arrives:

```ts
// components/CoverageMatrix.tsx (excerpt)
async function runCase(caseId: string, onEvent: (e: {event: string; data: any}) => void) {
  const res = await fetch('/api/run', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ caseId }),
  })
  const reader = res.body!.getReader()
  const dec = new TextDecoder()
  let buf = ''
  for (;;) {
    const { value, done } = await reader.read()
    if (done) break
    buf += dec.decode(value, { stream: true })
    const frames = buf.split('\n\n'); buf = frames.pop() ?? ''
    for (const f of frames) {
      const event = f.match(/^event: (.*)$/m)?.[1]
      const data  = f.match(/^data: (.*)$/m)?.[1]
      if (!event || !data) continue          // skip ": ping" heartbeats
      onEvent({ event, data: JSON.parse(data) })
    }
  }
}
// setState on each event → React re-renders the row for that criterion id → live fill
```

---

## 3. Env vars on Vercel (server-only secrets)

Any variable **without** the `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix is server-only and never enters the browser bundle **[DOC — Next.js env var semantics]**. So `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` stay secret by simply not prefixing them. Never read them in a `'use client'` file; read them only in `lib/llm/client.ts` and the route handler.

Setting them with the CLI (project already linked, authenticated as zkasuran) **[DOC — https://vercel.com/docs/cli/env, updated 2026-08-20]**:

```bash
# interactive (prompts for the value, hides it from shell history)
vercel env add OPENAI_API_KEY production
vercel env add ANTHROPIC_API_KEY production      # optional provider
vercel env add NEATLOGS_API_KEY production

# non-interactive, explicitly a Secret, no prompt
vercel env add OPENAI_API_KEY production --sensitive --value "sk-..." --yes

# from a file as the value (keeps the secret out of bash history — preferred over `echo |`)
vercel env add OPENAI_API_KEY production < ./openai.key

vercel env ls                                     # verify what is set, per environment
```

Add to `preview` too if you demo from a preview URL. Production vars default to type `secret` **[DOC]**. The docs explicitly warn that `echo value | vercel env add` saves the value in bash history, so use the interactive prompt or `< file` for keys **[DOC]**.

For local dev, pull them into an untracked file **[DOC]**:
```bash
vercel env pull .env.local            # development env by default
```

---

## 4. Timeout limits and keeping the agent under them

**[DOC — https://vercel.com/docs/functions/configuring-functions/duration, updated 2026-08-24]**, with Fluid compute (enabled by default on new projects):

| Plan | Default | Maximum | Extended |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hobby | 300s | **300s (5 min)** | — |
| Pro | 300s | **800s** | 1800s (30 min), beta |
| Enterprise | 300s | 800s | 1800s, beta |

Configured in App Router with the named export `export const maxDuration = 300` in the route file **[DOC]**.

**[FLAG]** these numbers assume Fluid compute is on (it is the default). If Fluid compute is disabled on the project, the older/shorter serverless limits apply and the agent can get cut off mid-run. Confirm Fluid compute is on in Project → Settings before the demo.

The limit that bites a live demo is the Hobby 300s ceiling, plus the docs' own warning that **idle** HTTP/1.1 connections can be dropped by intermediaries. Mitigations, in priority order:

1. **Stream incrementally (primary).** TTFB is tiny because `criteria_parsed` emits almost immediately and every `criterion_resolved` is pushed the instant it resolves. The matrix is visibly filling long before the function would ever hit its ceiling, so even a slow total run reads as "working," not "hung."
2. **Heartbeat every ~15s** (`: ping` comment frames) so an idle stretch between LLM calls does not look idle to the network **[DOC rationale]**.
3. **Cap criteria** for the demo (`maxCriteria: 12`). Bounds worst-case wall-clock.
4. **Parallelize the two evidence passes** per criterion with `Promise.all` (already in the sketch) to roughly halve per-criterion latency.
5. **Per-call timeout + global budget [INF].** Give each LLM call an `AbortController` timeout (e.g. 25s) and track a soft budget; if the budget is nearly spent, emit remaining criteria as a `deferred` verdict rather than blocking past the function ceiling.
6. Keep `runtime='nodejs'`. Edge runtime has different, shorter constraints and the OpenAI/Anthropic SDKs expect Node **[INF; I did not pull exact Edge limits — [FLAG]]**.

Set a project-wide default in `vercel.json` if you prefer not to annotate each route **[DOC]**:
```json
{ "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "functions": { "app/api/**/*": { "maxDuration": 300 } } }
```

---

## 5. Content-Security-Policy and security headers (Next production)

landing.md's Vite plugin does not apply. The Next-native approach is a **nonce-based CSP generated per request in the proxy/middleware file**, with the static (non-nonce) headers in `next.config`. **[DOC — https://nextjs.org/docs/app/guides/content-security-policy, Next 16.4.0]**

**[FLAG — file name is version-dependent]** On **Next 16** the file is **`proxy.ts`** exporting `proxy()` (this is what `create-next-app` scaffolds in Oct 2026, and what the current docs show). On **Next 13.4–15** it is **`middleware.ts`** exporting `middleware()`, with an identical body. Rename the file and the function; nothing else changes.

**Tradeoff to accept consciously [DOC]:** a nonce forces **dynamic rendering** on every page (no static optimization, no CDN caching, PPR incompatible), because the nonce is injected during SSR from the request's CSP header. For PriorProof this is fine, the app is an interactive live demo, not a cacheable marketing page. If you later need the landing page statically cached, the alternative is Next's experimental hash-based CSP via Subresource Integrity (`experimental.sri`) which keeps static generation **[DOC]**.

```ts
// proxy.ts  (Next 16;  rename to middleware.ts / middleware() on <=15)
import { NextRequest, NextResponse } from 'next/server'

export function proxy(request: NextRequest) {
  const nonce = Buffer.from(crypto.randomUUID()).toString('base64')
  const isDev = process.env.NODE_ENV === 'development'
  const csp = `
    default-src 'self';
    script-src 'self' 'nonce-${nonce}' 'strict-dynamic'${isDev ? " 'unsafe-eval'" : ''};
    style-src 'self' ${isDev ? "'unsafe-inline'" : `'nonce-${nonce}'`};
    img-src 'self' blob: data:;
    font-src 'self';
    connect-src 'self';
    object-src 'none';
    base-uri 'self';
    form-action 'self';
    frame-ancestors 'none';
    upgrade-insecure-requests;
  `.replace(/\s{2,}/g, ' ').trim()

  const requestHeaders = new Headers(request.headers)
  requestHeaders.set('x-nonce', nonce)
  requestHeaders.set('Content-Security-Policy', csp)
  const res = NextResponse.next({ request: { headers: requestHeaders } })
  res.headers.set('Content-Security-Policy', csp)
  return res
}

export const config = {
  matcher: [{
    source: '/((?!api|_next/static|_next/image|favicon.ico).*)',
    missing: [
      { type: 'header', key: 'next-router-prefetch' },
      { type: 'header', key: 'purpose', value: 'prefetch' },
    ],
  }],
}
```

Notes: `connect-src 'self'` explicitly allows the same-origin `fetch('/api/run')` stream (it would also fall back to `default-src 'self'`). The matcher deliberately excludes `/api`, so the CSP's nonce machinery never touches the SSE endpoint (which returns `text/event-stream`, not HTML) — correct. Next auto-attaches the nonce to its own framework scripts and to `<Script nonce={nonce}>` read via `headers()` **[DOC]**.

Static headers (apply to every response including `/api` and static assets) go in `next.config` — do **not** also put CSP here, to avoid a conflicting second policy:

```ts
// next.config.ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'
const securityHeaders = [
  { key: 'X-Content-Type-Options', value: 'nosniff' },
  { key: 'Referrer-Policy', value: 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' },
  { key: 'X-Frame-Options', value: 'DENY' },                 // legacy clickjacking fallback; frame-ancestors 'none' is the modern one in the CSP
  { key: 'Strict-Transport-Security', value: 'max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload' },
  { key: 'Permissions-Policy', value: 'camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), browsing-topics=()' },
  { key: 'X-DNS-Prefetch-Control', value: 'off' },
]
const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  async headers() {
    return [{ source: '/:path*', headers: securityHeaders }]
  },
}
export default nextConfig
```

**[INF]** HSTS `preload` is only appropriate once you are certain the apex and all subdomains are HTTPS-only; on a throwaway `*.vercel.app` demo you may drop `preload`. Vercel serves HTTPS and sets HSTS on its own domains anyway.

---

## 6. Deploy commands (CLI already authenticated as zkasuran)

**[DOC — https://vercel.com/docs/cli/deploying-from-cli, updated 2026-09-08]**

```bash
# 1. link this directory to a Vercel project (creates .vercel/)
vercel link

# 2. attach secrets BEFORE deploy (see §3), then confirm
vercel env add OPENAI_API_KEY production
vercel env add NEATLOGS_API_KEY production
vercel env ls

# 3. pull project settings + env locally so a local build matches prod
vercel pull --environment=production      # writes to .vercel/

# 4a. simple path — build on Vercel and promote to production
vercel --prod

# 4b. or prebuilt path — build locally, inspect .vercel/output, then upload
vercel build
vercel deploy --prebuilt --prod
```

**[DOC]** the first deploy of a brand-new project is always a production deploy even without `--prod`; later deploys need `--prod` to hit production (otherwise they are preview). `vercel pull` (not `vercel env pull`) is the one to use alongside `vercel build`/`vercel dev` because it writes both settings and env into `.vercel/` **[DOC]**.

---

## Confirmed vs inferred, and open flags

Confirmed from docs just now: route-handler `ReadableStream` streaming and the async-iterator pattern; `maxDuration` named export; the Hobby/Pro/Enterprise duration table (300s Hobby max, 800s Pro, 1800s beta) under Fluid compute; the idle-connection/heartbeat warning; nonce CSP via proxy/middleware and its forced-dynamic-rendering tradeoff; SRI alternative; all `vercel env` / `vercel link` / `vercel pull` / `vercel --prod` / `vercel deploy --prebuilt` syntax.

Inferred (reasoning given, not line-item in docs): import-fixtures-over-fs for bundle tracing; `fetch`-reader over `EventSource` because of POST; `X-Accel-Buffering: no` and `no-transform` as anti-buffering belt-and-suspenders; per-call `AbortController` budget; Node over Edge runtime choice.
